concepts.def: The four 'rightly guided' caliphs - Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali - who led the Muslim community from 632 to 661.
The Prophet's close companion and first caliph, who held the community together through the Riddah wars and began gathering the Qur'an.
The second caliph, under whom Muslim rule expanded into Syria, Egypt and Persia, and strong administrative systems were established.
The third caliph, who had a standard written text of the Qur'an prepared and sent to the provinces; he was killed by rebels in 656.
The Prophet's cousin and son-in-law, whose caliphate was marked by the first civil war within Islam and who was assassinated in 661.
Disagreement over rightful leadership: Shi'a Muslims hold that Ali was the Prophet's designated successor, while Sunnis accept the order of the four caliphs.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Islam: The Four Rightly Guided Caliphs — a core area of GCSE Religious Studies.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Islam: The Four Rightly Guided Caliphs brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Islam: The Four Rightly Guided Caliphs.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Who became the first caliph after the death of the Prophet Muhammad?
options: Abu Bakr
Ali
Umar
Uthman

mcqs.q: Which caliph had a standard written text of the Qur'an prepared and distributed?
options: Uthman
Abu Bakr
Umar
Ali

mcqs.q: Under which caliph did Muslim rule expand into Syria, Egypt and Persia?
options: Umar
Abu Bakr
Ali
Muawiyah

mcqs.q: What was Ali's relationship to the Prophet Muhammad?
options: His cousin and son-in-law, married to Fatimah
His brother
His uncle
No family relationship

mcqs.q: Were the four caliphs prophets like Muhammad?
options: No - they were leaders of the community, not prophets; Muslims believe Muhammad was the final prophet, the 'Seal of the Prophets'.
The caliphs were Byzantine governors appointed by the emperor.
The succession was decided by the Roman senate.
Each caliph was a new prophet who received revelation.

mcqs.q: Did all Muslims agree about the succession to the Prophet?
options: No - those who became the Shi'a believed Ali had been designated as successor, while others accepted Abu Bakr; this dispute underlies the Sunni-Shi'a division.
The caliphs were Byzantine governors appointed by the emperor.
The choice of Abu Bakr was accepted unanimously without any disagreement.
The succession was decided by the Roman senate.

mcqs.q: Was the era of the four caliphs free of conflict?
options: The succession was decided by the Roman senate.
The Rashidun period was a perfectly peaceful golden age.
The four caliphs all died peacefully of old age.
No - three of the four caliphs were assassinated, and Ali's reign saw the first civil war; 'rightly guided' expresses religious respect, not an absence of strife.

The Prophet's cousin and son-in-law, whose caliphate was marked by the first civil war within Islam and who was assassinated in 661.
